newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Brit Gas hit by exceptional charges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brit Gas hit by exceptional charges.

text.p: British Gas Plc on Thursday reported it fell deeper into the red in the third quarter mainly because of exceptional costs for expected losses on gas supply contracts.
The privatised utility took a total charge of 304 million pounds ($510 million), producing a third quarter net loss of 364 million pounds compared with 181 million a year ago.

British Gas said the bulk of the exceptional charge, 294 million pounds, was the indirect result of the so-called take-or-pay contracts which oblige it to buy more gas from North Sea gas producers than it wants.

British Gas is seeking to renegotiate such deals, made at a time when there was virtually no free market in such sales. They oblige the utility to buy gas from North Sea producers at prices well above market rates.

It was forced to seek to unravel the crippling long-term contracts last year in the face of a falling share of the increasingly competitive U.K. gas market and tumbling spot gas prices since deregulation began.
To reduce the surplus British Gas agreed to supply continental companies on loss-making terms once the Interconnector pipeline between Britain and Europe is completed in 1998.
British Gas said it made more sense to sell some of the surplus gas below cost price to the continent than store it in Britain where it would not yield any money at all.
"It is better to make a loss in signing these contracts than face the bigger loss of accumulating a large surplus of gas that cannot be sold," Hampton said.
He added British Gas was making good progress in renegotiating the burdensome take-or-pay contracts, but warned that more exceptional charges were inevitable as a result.
"We should be able to achieve something in the relatively near term," he said. "(But) when we conclude the renegotiations of the North Sea contracts, inevitably there will be a charge."
Hampton declined to elaborate on recent speculation that oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group had at some stage considered taking over British Gas.
"We have nothing to say about potential takeovers. We are still on track to achieve the demerger by the originally announced timetable," he said.

British Gas aims to split itself into separate trading and transport firms in the spring of 1997 and is currently embroiled in a Monopolies and Mergers Commission inquiry into the price regime governing its transport arm. It booked 10 million pounds in exceptional charges for the planned break-up.

The company benefited from increased demand in the third quarter following colder weather than a year ago. But it added low spot gas prices continued to hurt its performance in the fiercely-competitive market for big industrial users.
This business suffered losses of about 90 million pounds compared with 70 million pounds in 1995's third quarter.
In the domestic market some 80,000 out of a total 500,000 customers switched to rivals after a pilot project to introduce competition started in the south west of England in April.
Overall trading losses widened marginally in the third quarter to 286 million pounds from 285 million.
"Our third quarter results are always dominated by the summer when people don't consume much, so the trading performance is never particularly interesting in that period," Hampton said.
British Gas' transport arm TransCo posted an operating profit of 88 million stg after a three million loss a year ago.
An additional 80 million sterling will be spent this year to address the problems with a new gas billing system, British Gas said after it faced a barrage of customer complaints earlier in the year.
Shares in British Gas were unperturbed by the third-quarter results, easing two pence to 219 pence in line with the overall market in late morning trade.
"We knew the provisions would have to be taken and we know there will be more," said Kleinwort Benson analyst Paul Spedding. ($1=.5956 Pound)
